project.deck: A RAG engine built to be measured

body.text: Strata-RAG is a retrieval-augmented generation engine I built and open-sourced. It has the parts you would expect: Qdrant with explicit HNSW parameters, hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval fused by reciprocal rank, a cross-encoder reranker, a metadata sidecar for questions that are really aggregations rather than searches, and an eval harness reporting Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR and nDCG separately from an LLM-judge faithfulness score.
That half is the easy half. The engine exists because of the other one.

I built it over a large heterogeneous production document corpus — real files, several formats, no shared convention between them. What that corpus surfaced was mostly not retrieval quality. It was content that should never have been indexed, and guardrails I had asserted but never measured.
What is actually inside your documents

Ingest-time redaction — entropy scoring plus contextual key detection — caught and redacted 174 live credentials before a single chunk was embedded. Once a secret is in a vector store the model can quote it back on request and there is no clean way to take it out again, so the only reliable place to stop it is upstream of the embedding call.

Two structural details matter more than the count. Secret redaction is a separate pass that runs before PII redaction, so an email:password pair is recognised as a credential instead of being anonymised into a harmless-looking email address. And the metadata harvest, which reads config files that are never embedded at all, pulls fields through a whitelist rather than a blocklist — so a secret block some future config introduces is excluded by default, not by a deny-list entry I would have to remember to add.
The red team that broke my own scanner

The prompt-injection scanner matched literal ASCII patterns against the bytes it was handed. I wrote a red team to attack it, and it lost badly: 93% of obfuscated payloads walked straight past — zero-width splits, homoglyphs, full-width characters, base64, and several more baroque encodings.

The fix is a normalisation pre-pass. The scanner now reads a normalised copy of the untrusted text (NFKC fold, strip zero-width characters, un-map homoglyphs, bounded base64/morse/rot13 decode-and-rescan) while the original bytes remain what the user is shown. Measured end to end: scanner evasion 93% → 17%, end-to-end attack success 58% → 8%, six fold/decode encoder families 100% → 0%.

The residual 17% is published rather than buried, its families named: acrostics, leetspeak, morse-encoded URLs, fragmented and triple-nested base64. The normaliser was promoted into the engine and the red team imports it from there, so defence and attack tooling share one reversible component and cannot quietly drift apart.
The metric needed a denominator, and the oracle needed no vocabulary

Live testing then found the same zero-width payload hijacking the model in six of eight trials, and refusing once. A single-shot attack-success rate is a coin flip presented as a measurement. The harness now fires each payload N times and reports a per-payload success rate, with errors — timeouts, 502s — excluded from the denominator: a failed request is not a refusal, and counting it as one flatters the defence. Scanner evasion stays single-shot, because that layer genuinely is a function of the bytes.

The harder half was the oracle that decides whether an answer means the attack worked. It went through five rewrites, and every lexical approach died on a reproduced counter-example. Substring matching scored a refusal that quotes the canary — “I will not output <canary>” — as a hijack. A proximity window fixed that and introduced cross-clause false negatives. Per-span negation scoping fixed those and still over-reported on needles quoted inside code fences. A refusal-taint rule was sound until it met the alerting register: “Disregarding…”, “blocked”, “I stay in my role”, refusals containing no negation word at all.

A negation lexicon is an unbounded arms race, so I deleted the vocabulary. The deterministic success path is structural only: it fires on forms a refusal physically cannot produce — the stripped answer is the bare token, an un-fenced image beacon owns its own line — and everything else goes to a behavioural LLM judge, or is scored conservatively when no judge is available. That buys the property worth five rewrites: the layer errs in a single direction, so a deterministic-only score is a documented conservative lower bound and never a false all-clear. The 11 false positives and 2 false negatives reproduced across those rounds are baked into the test suite as permanent regressions.

Some choices here are argued rather than measured, and the record says so. Hybrid retrieval is one: a cosine score and a BM25 score live on incomparable scales, which is the whole reason reciprocal-rank fusion combines them by rank position instead of by number. The reasoning is sound, and the dense-only A/B on the real corpus has not been run, so the claim carries no figure. There is a --dense-only flag whose purpose is to settle it later.

The injection work merged only after an independent review panel that had not written the code found three major and four minor real defects sitting behind 441 passing tests. Green tests were the floor, not the verdict.
Strata-RAG is on GitHub at github.com/NikolaiSachok/Strata-RAG, with the design decisions and the residual failures documented next to the code.
